title: Tenant‑prioritized prefill queue and cross‑HW decode pacing
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem statement:

High-concurrency multi-tenant traffic causes bursts of prefill work that compete for limited KV slots and decoder throughput across heterogeneous accelerators (A100-like vs L4-like). Current admission is coarse: first-come batches can evict active tenant KV pages and stall low‑latency requests. Kernels and decode pipelines on different HW have varying decode throughput and latency distributions, which makes naive batching and prefill pumping unpredictable.

Goal:

Design and implement a tenant-prioritized prefill admission queue with HW-aware decode pacing to: (1) reduce eviction churn for active tenants, (2) provide predictable latency SLOs for high‑priority routes, and (3) improve overall token efficiency by aligning prefill work to kernel & accelerator capability.

Success metrics:

- 20% reduction in KV eviction rate during 95th-percentile burst windows for tenants with "priority" label
- 15% median end-to-end prefill latency improvement for P0 routes under 95th-percentile load
- No regression (>2%) in aggregate tokens/sec throughput across clusters

Design overview (high level):

1) Per-tenant prefilling queues: maintain lightweight in-memory admission queues per tenant/keyspace. Each queue exposes a small configurable priority weight. Prefill requests are classified at ingress and enqueued rather than immediately prefilled if backlog > soft_threshold.

2) Admission controller with budget tokens: each tenant has a refill budget (tokens) representing allowed concurrent prefill in flight; budgets are replenished via a leaky-bucket tied to recent success and observed KV hit-rate. Budgets prevent runaway multi-tenant prefill storms.

3) Kernel & accelerator capability descriptor: expose a small capability vector for each HW class (decode_tps_estimate, single_step_latency_ns, preferred_batch_sizes). Runtime uses the vector to decide target batch sizes and decode pump rate per hardware.

4) Cross-HW decode pacing: implement a pump per HW class that pulls from tenant queues respecting tenant budgets and kernel capability. The pump schedules prefill batches to match the HW's preferred batch sizes and avoids overdriving low-latency HW during high-priority route windows.

5) Soft reservations for hot KV slots: allow tenants above a hotness threshold to maintain soft reservations (small fraction of KV slot pool) to prevent eviction of active session pages. Reservations are revocable when global pressure is high.

6) Fragmentation-aware coalescer: when allocating small KV fragments, the allocator attempts to coalesce small adjacent fragments at enqueue time (cheap heuristics) and defers physical compaction to off-peak windows.

7) Telemetry & fallback: surface queue lengths, budget exhaustion events, actual batch sizes, per‑HW pump utilization, eviction incidents. On severe overload, fallback policy is to reject non‑P0 prefill requests with a 429-like signal upstream and fall back to partial KV reconstruction on host CPU when possible.

Implementation phases:

Phase 1 (spike, 1 week): implement in-memory per-tenant queue + budget model; add simulation harness to replay production prefill traces (sampled) and run micro-sim with tunable HW capability vectors.

Phase 2 (engineer-safe deploy, 2 sprints): implement admission controller and per-HW pumps in runtime; introduce metrics and control plane knobs (soft_thresholds, budget rates). Add unit + integration tests.

Phase 3 (canary + rollout, 2 weeks): deploy to a single region with canary routing for low-volume high-priority tenants. Collect SLO telemetry and iterate.

Acceptance criteria (engineering):

- Integration tests covering budget exhaustion and multi-tenant fairness scenarios
- Simulation demonstrates expected eviction reduction on sampled traces
- Canary must show no increase in 99th p99 prefill latency for P0 routes before scaling rollout

Trade-offs and open questions:

- Complexity vs observability: adding per-tenant state increases memory and control-plane complexity; mitigate with soft limits and TTL eviction of inactive queues.
- Reservation fairness: soft reservations favor steady tenants; must avoid starvation for new tenants — implement fairness decay and cross-tenant arbitration.
- Kernel descriptor staleness: HW capability descriptors may be approximations; we will start with conservative defaults and expose a tuning endpoint for SRE.

Implementation notes / pointers:

- Simulation harness: link to sandbox repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/prefill-sim (PR will be created ENG-238401-prefill-sim)
- Design doc draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=7890123
- Related perf dashboard: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/prefill/prefill-eviction-overview
- Expected PR patterns: runtime changes behind feature-flag "tenant_prefill_q_v1", control-plane knobs via config service.
comments: 2026-03-02 - Aisha Kapoor: Spike started. Collected 24h sampled prefill traces from prod (1% sample). Identified two dominant failure modes: (a) eviction storms triggered by large background batch warmups, (b) low-latency routes that experience prefill starvation during bursts.
2026-03-04 - Liam O'Connor: Implemented baseline per-tenant queue and simple token bucket. Local sim shows 18% eviction reduction on sample trace with conservative budget defaults.
2026-03-06 - Review (Marta Ruiz): Requested clarifications on soft reservation revocation policy and metrics. Recommending adding \"reservation_revocations\" and \"reservation_reclaims\" counters.

2026-03-08 - Liam O'Connor: Added pump prototype for two HW classes (high-throughput, low-latency). Observed misprediction when matching batch sizes; will add an adaptive probe that adjusts target batch size for next window.
2026-03-10 - Aisha Kapoor: Decided to gate rollout behind feature flag and add a canary that targets 5 tenants with p0 routes. Next: infra change to surface per-tenant queue TTL and GC.
